title: NURS 1017 Unit 5 Case Study 7

question.stem: Which findings require immediate follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lesions stop at the midline
Vesicle on the tip of the nose
Temperature 37.9° C
Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
Provides daytime care for her 4-month-old grandson
Left-eye redness, sensitivity to light, and blurred vision
Blood pressure 146/84 mm Hg
Takes methotrexate weekly and prednisone daily
Had chickenpox as a child
Pain rated 8/10, burning, worse with light touch

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.explanation:
Correct answers: the vesicle on the tip of the nose (Option 2), the left-eye redness, sensitivity to light and blurred vision (Option 6), methotrexate and prednisone (Option 8), daytime care of her 4-month-old grandson (Option 5), and pain 8/10 that is worse with light touch (Option 10).

Why these need immediate follow-up

  • Vesicle on the tip of the nose (Option 2): the Hutchinson sign. The nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic (V1) division of the trigeminal nerve supplies both the tip of the nose and the eye, so eye involvement is likely. The provider is informed immediately of any facial lesion, especially near the eye or ear.
  • Red eye, photophobia, blurred vision (Option 6): signs of ocular involvement (conjunctivitis, keratitis, uveitis) that can threaten sight and need urgent ophthalmology assessment.
  • Methotrexate and prednisone (Option 8): immunosuppression raises the risk of severe, prolonged or disseminated zoster. It changes the treatment setting (IV antiviral), the isolation needed and the monitoring.
  • Cares for a 4-month-old (Option 5): the infant is too young for varicella vaccination and could develop chickenpox from contact with lesion fluid. This needs immediate teaching and exposure planning.
  • Pain 8/10 with allodynia (Option 10): zoster pain is often moderate to severe. Severe acute pain needs prompt treatment and is linked to a higher risk of postherpetic neuralgia.

Why the others do not

  • Lesions stop at the midline (Option 1) and grouped vesicles on a red base (Option 4): expected features of zoster: vesicular, dermatomal, on one side, never crossing the midline.
  • Childhood chickenpox (Option 9): explains why zoster occurred (reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus); no immediate action.
  • Temperature 37.9° C (Option 3): low-grade fever and malaise fit the viral prodrome; continue to monitor.
  • BP 146/84 mm Hg (Option 7): mildly elevated, likely from pain and stress; recheck after the pain is treated.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it is an expected manifestation of herpes zoster, suggests ocular (eye) involvement, or increases the risk of severe or complicated disease.

rows.text: Burning, tingling pain for 3 days before the rash appeared
Lesions limited to one side, stopping at the midline
Vesicle on the tip of the nose
Photophobia and blurred vision in the left eye

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.preamble: Phase 1 — Primary Care Clinic, 1030. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1030.
question.explanation:
Correct answers

  • Expected manifestation: burning, tingling pain for 3 days before the rash; lesions limited to one side, stopping at the midline; low-grade fever and fatigue.
  • Suggests ocular involvement: vesicle on the tip of the nose; photophobia and blurred vision in the left eye.
  • Increases the risk of severe disease: daily prednisone and weekly methotrexate; age 72.

Why

  • Prodromal burning pain: a burning or tingling sensation where the rash appears several days later is the typical prodrome.
  • One side, stopping at the midline: zoster follows a single dermatome (the area supplied by one nerve root) and does not cross the midline.
  • Low-grade fever and fatigue: part of the prodrome (feeling unwell, fever).
  • Vesicle on the nose tip: the Hutchinson sign. The nasociliary nerve supplies both the nose tip and the eye, so this strongly predicts eye involvement.
  • Photophobia and blurred vision: suggest corneal or intraocular inflammation.
  • Prednisone and methotrexate: suppress the cell-mediated immunity that normally keeps the virus dormant, raising the risk of dissemination and prolonged viral shedding.
  • Age 72: zoster most often affects older adults, and age raises the risk of complications, including postherpetic neuralgia.

Beyond the chapter: the Hutchinson sign and the immunosuppression risk are standard content.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The nurse's priority is to prevent [[drop0]] because [[drop1]]. The nurse's immediate action should be to [[drop2]]. The nurse also recognizes the client's [[drop3]] as a concurrent priority.

options.text: secondary bacterial skin infection
hyperglycemia
permanent vision loss
scarring of the forehead
the client is older than 65 years
the virus is affecting the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
the client had chickenpox as a child
the lesions are vesicular
teach the client to apply warm compresses to the eye
apply antibiotic ointment to the left eyelid
schedule a follow-up visit in 1 week
notify the provider immediately so that urgent ophthalmology assessment can be arranged
fluid volume excess
acute pain
hypothermia
impaired gas exchange

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: The nurse's priority is to prevent permanent vision loss because the virus is affecting the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. The nurse's immediate action should be to notify the provider immediately so that urgent ophthalmology assessment can be arranged. The nurse also recognizes the client's acute pain as a concurrent priority.

Why

  • Permanent vision loss: herpes zoster ophthalmicus can cause keratitis, uveitis, glaucoma and vision loss. A threat of permanent loss of function takes priority over skin integrity; zoster on facial dermatomes can affect eyesight and hearing.
  • Ophthalmic (V1) division: the forehead, scalp, upper eyelid and nose-tip lesions map to V1, which explains why the eye is at risk.
  • Notify the provider immediately: facial lesions near the eye or ear are reported at once. Putting ointment in or near the eye or applying warm compresses without a prescription is outside the nurse's scope and could cause harm; waiting a week risks permanent damage.
  • Acute pain: pain rated 8/10 with allodynia must be treated promptly; adequate pain control is a recognized priority in zoster care.

Why the other choices do not fit

  • Secondary skin infection, scarring and hyperglycemia are possible later problems but not the most urgent threat. Her age, the vesicles and childhood chickenpox do not explain why the eye is at risk. Fluid volume excess, impaired gas exchange and hypothermia are not supported by the data.

question.stem: The nurse plans care for the client on the medical unit. Which five interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select five.

options.text: Gently open intact vesicles to help the lesions dry faster
Infuse each acyclovir dose over at least 1 hour, maintain hydration, and keep strict intake and output
Place the client in an airborne infection isolation room and use airborne and contact precautions
Hold the client's daily prednisone to improve her immune response
Tell the daughter she may bring the baby to visit if she wears a gown and gloves
Monitor the serum creatinine daily
Give the recombinant shingles vaccine now to shorten this episode
Apply the prescribed mupirocin ointment to the left eye and eyelid margin
Assign staff members with documented immunity to varicella
Assess left-eye symptoms and visual acuity each shift and report changes

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.preamble: Phase 2 — Medical Unit, Same Day 1400. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1400 and the Provider Orders.
question.explanation:
Correct answers: airborne infection isolation room with airborne and contact precautions (Option 3), staff with documented immunity to varicella (Option 9), acyclovir over at least 1 hour with hydration and strict intake and output (Option 2), left-eye assessment each shift (Option 10), and daily serum creatinine (Option 6).

Why these five

  • Airborne and contact precautions (Option 3): for localized zoster in an immunocompromised client, isolation guidance calls for airborne and contact precautions until disseminated infection is ruled out (matches the provider's order).
  • Immune staff (Option 9): varicella-zoster virus spreads to people who are not immune; non-immune or pregnant staff should not provide care.
  • Slow acyclovir infusion, hydration, intake and output (Option 2): IV acyclovir can precipitate as crystals in the renal tubules and cause acute kidney injury, especially with rapid infusion or dehydration.
  • Eye assessment (Option 10): follows from the priority of preventing vision loss; worsening vision is reported promptly to ophthalmology.
  • Daily creatinine (Option 6): detects acyclovir-related kidney injury early.

Why not the others

  • Baby visits with gown and gloves (Option 5): the 4-month-old is unvaccinated against varicella and the client is on airborne precautions; a gown and gloves do not protect the infant.
  • Opening intact vesicles (Option 1): increases the risk of secondary bacterial infection and scarring.
  • Mupirocin in the eye (Option 8): the order is for skin lesions only. Only ophthalmic preparations go in the eye.
  • Holding prednisone (Option 4): stopping long-term corticosteroids abruptly risks adrenal insufficiency; the provider continued it, and any change needs a prescriber's order.
  • Shingles vaccine now (Option 7): the vaccine prevents future episodes; it does not treat active zoster. Vaccination is discussed after recovery.

Beyond the chapter: isolation details follow CDC and Public Health Agency of Canada guidance; acyclovir nephrotoxicity is standard pharmacology.

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: Before entering the client's room, the nurse performs hand hygiene and dons a gown, gloves, and a fit-tested N95 respirator. The door to the client's room must remain closed. Before the client is transported to the eye clinic for her slit-lamp examination, the nurse places a surgical mask on the client and prepares her by covering the skin lesions with a clean dressing. After administering the prescribed oxycodone for pain rated 8/10, the nurse plans to reassess pain within 60 minutes.

Why

  • Fit-tested N95 respirator: airborne precautions require an N95 (or higher) respirator; a surgical mask does not filter airborne particles adequately.
  • Door closed: an airborne infection isolation room keeps its negative pressure only while the door is closed. Leaving it open for observation defeats the room.
  • Surgical mask on the client: during essential transport, the client wears a surgical mask to contain her respiratory secretions. An N95 is not placed on a client: it is designed to protect the wearer, and some have an exhalation valve.
  • Covering the skin lesions: limits contact and airborne spread from vesicle fluid. Mupirocin is for skin lesions only, never the eye.
  • Reassess pain within 60 minutes: reassessing within the drug's peak time (about 30 to 60 minutes for oral opioids, per agency policy) evaluates pain relief and sedation. Waiting until the next dose leaves uncontrolled pain unnoticed.

Beyond the chapter: transmission-based precaution details follow the CDC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions; Public Health Agency of Canada guidance is consistent.

question.stem: The nurse reviews the hospital day 4 flowsheet. Highlight the findings that indicate the client's condition or understanding has not progressed as expected and requires follow-up.
question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.preamble: Phase 3 — Medical Unit, Hospital Day 4. The nurse has reviewed the Hospital Day 4 Flowsheet.
question.explanation:
Highlight these three findings: serum creatinine 163 µmol/L (admission 78 µmol/L); intake 1,600 mL with urine output 380 mL; and the statement “Once the scabs are gone, any burning that's left doesn't mean anything, so I won't bother anyone about it.”

Why these need follow-up

  • Creatinine more than doubled: suggests acyclovir-associated acute kidney injury. The nurse notifies the provider promptly; the dose may need adjusting and hydration reviewed.
  • Urine output 380 mL in 24 hours: oliguria (under about 400 mL/24 h, or under 0.5 mL/kg/h; for a 60-kg client, at least 720 mL/24 h is expected) despite an adequate intake supports kidney injury.
  • "Any burning that's left doesn't mean anything": pain that persists after the rash heals may be postherpetic neuralgia, a treatable neurological complication that should be reported. The teaching needs reinforcing.

Why the others show expected progress

  • Temperature 37.0° C, all lesions crusted with no new lesions, pain 3/10 and a stable eye: afebrile, no dissemination, pain controlled. Once all lesions are crusted, she is no longer considered infectious.
  • Capillary glucose 7.4 mmol/L: acceptable for a client with diabetes taking prednisone.
  • The vaccine and hand-hygiene statements are accurate. The recombinant (non-live) zoster vaccine is recommended after recovery, including for people who are immunocompromised (NACI; CDC).

Beyond the chapter: acyclovir nephrotoxicity and the vaccine recommendations are standard references.

description: A 72-year-old immunosuppressed female client with herpes zoster involving the left forehead, scalp, and eye, from the primary care clinic through hospitalization and discharge planning.
